To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) acute stimulation of dorsal hippocampal cells that were active during fear memory formation drove place avoidance behavior, while acute stimulation of ventral hippocampus cells that were active while encoding fear memory formation drove a context-specific place preference; and (2) chronic stimulation of dorsal hippocampus fear memory produced context-specific reduction in fear responses, while chronic stimulation of ventral fear memory produced context specific enhancement of fear responses

1) Optically tagging and stimulating cells in the dorsal and ventral regions of the hippocampus acutely, but not chronically, drive place avoidance and place preference behaviors; 2) Chronic stimulation of dorsal and ventral fear memories differentially modulate fear expression; 3) The behavioral expression of fear memory is modulated by the hippocampus and basolateral amyglada, but not the medial prefrontal cortex.
